title: Unit Testing with xUnit and pytest
oneLiner: Writing your first unit tests: arrange, act, assert, xUnit's Fact and Theory next to pytest functions and parametrize, testing for exceptions, per-test setup with constructors and fixtures, running the tests and reading failures.
keyTakeaway: A unit test calls one small piece of code with chosen inputs and asserts the result. Test the boundaries and the errors, not just the happy path; keep tests independent (fresh data for each); compare floats with a tolerance; and run the whole suite on every change, with dotnet test or pytest.
explanation:
A unit test is a small, automatic check of one piece of your code: call this function with these inputs and assert that the result is that. A good set of tests runs in seconds and tells you immediately when a change breaks something that used to work, which is what lets teams change code confidently.

The lesson writes the same tests twice: with xUnit, the most widely used C# test framework, and pytest, the most widely used Python one. Both find your tests by convention, run each one separately, and report exactly which assertion failed with what values. You'll see single tests, parametrized tests that run the same check over a table of inputs, tests that check an exception is raised, and per-test setup (an xUnit constructor, a pytest test fixture).

Test frameworks can't run inside the exercise editor, so the framework samples were run with dotnet test and pytest for this lesson and are meant for your own projects, while the predict-the-output questions use plain code to show the ideas: boundaries, tolerances for floats, error messages and test isolation. Every graded exercise in this app is itself a set of unit tests run against your code.
